label: CAMPAIGN 05
title: The Language of the Economy
firewall: We track how the words have been used and how fast they are winning, not whether the underlying politics is correct.
summary: One economy, three names — and with all seventeen terms now measured against full-text coverage, the gap between the data and the mood is legible in the velocities. When inflation re-accelerated to a three-year high while markets hit records, the same economy acquired three incompatible vocabularies — the institutional one that measures a rate, the lived-experience one that feels a price level, and the political one that assigns a blame. Measured, it is the lived-experience vocabulary that is running away with the cycle: 'vibecession' is the fastest mover in the set, up 573 percent over thirty days at velocity 100, and 'shrinkflation' (velocity 94, up 180 percent over thirty days) and 'are you better off' (velocity 81) are close behind, while the institutional-optimism word 'soft landing' has faded to velocity 19, down 28 percent on the quarter. Year-over-year change is not computed this cycle — the full-text series runs a 180-day window — so every figure here is 30-day and 90-day momentum.
anchor: June 2026: consumer inflation hit a three-year high on an energy-and-tariff shock, even as equity markets set records and roughly two of three households reported cutting back — with a Fed leadership handoff and the 2026 midterms underneath. The data and the lived experience point in opposite directions, and three vocabularies have formed to name the gap.
thesis: One economy, three names — and with all seventeen terms now measured against full-text coverage, the gap between the data and the mood is legible in the velocities. When inflation re-accelerated to a three-year high while markets hit records, the same economy acquired three incompatible vocabularies — the institutional one that measures a rate, the lived-experience one that feels a price level, and the political one that assigns a blame. Measured, it is the lived-experience vocabulary that is running away with the cycle: 'vibecession' is the fastest mover in the set, up 573 percent over thirty days at velocity 100, and 'shrinkflation' (velocity 94, up 180 percent over thirty days) and 'are you better off' (velocity 81) are close behind, while the institutional-optimism word 'soft landing' has faded to velocity 19, down 28 percent on the quarter. Year-over-year change is not computed this cycle — the full-text series runs a 180-day window — so every figure here is 30-day and 90-day momentum.

The defining tension is 'soft landing' versus 'vibecession': the institutional-optimism vocabulary is fading exactly as the lived-experience vocabulary surges, the same data-turning producing opposite vocabulary movements. The one institutional term gaining is not the reassuring one — 'higher for longer' is up 207 percent over ninety days (velocity 38), so the market's own message is not that the landing was soft but that rates will stay high. Contextive tracks how fast each name is winning, not whether the economy is actually good or bad; that the vibe word is winning the argument the data word is presumed to be winning is a statement about momentum, not a verdict on the print.

definingTension.note: The cycle's defining collision, and it is measured. As inflation re-accelerated, the institutional-optimism term faded while the lived-pessimism term surged — the same data-turning producing opposite vocabulary movements. 'Vibecession' is the fastest mover in the set (velocity 100, up 573 percent over thirty days and up 7 percent on the quarter) while 'soft landing' has fallen to velocity 19, down 28 percent over ninety days. The vibe word is winning the argument the data word is presumed to be winning: the feeling is outrunning the rate.

clusters.name: Lived-experience / populist
clusters.blurb: How the economy is named from the checkout line — the feeling is the fact, a price level not a rate. It moves fastest when official data improves while prices stay high, because that gap is the vocabulary's whole territory.

clusters.name: Institutional / macro
clusters.blurb: The vocabulary of the Fed, the analyst class, and the markets desk — engineered for precision: a rate, a target, a path. Technically correct and rhetorically losing when the rate and the level diverge.

clusters.name: Political-blame
clusters.blurb: The vocabulary that converts the economy into a verdict — attribution devices that assign a cause and a culprit. Symmetric: every term has been deployed by whichever coalition is out of power.

pillars.title: The vocabulary of an economy that doesn't feel like the data
pillars.body: Cluster A against the inflation print — 'vibecession,' 'affordability,' 'shrinkflation,' 'greedflation' — using the data-vs-vibes gap as the spine. Measured, this is the loudest cluster: 'vibecession' tops the set (velocity 100, up 573 percent over thirty days), 'shrinkflation' is close behind (velocity 94, up 180 percent over thirty days and 46 percent on the quarter), 'greedflation' holds high (velocity 88) and 'price gouging' is up 94 percent on the quarter (velocity 62). The highest-recognition piece; every reader has paid the prices, and the numbers say the words for paying them are the ones winning.

pillars.title: One number, three vocabularies
pillars.body: A single inflation print as the unit of analysis, tracking how the rate vocabulary, the level vocabulary, and the blame vocabulary name the same figure. The cycle's most analytical argument: a rate and a level are different objects, and the velocities show the level vocabulary ('affordability,' 'cost-of-living crisis' up 57 percent on the quarter) outrunning the rate vocabulary ('disinflation' down 28 percent, 'soft landing' down 28 percent). Even the institutional cluster's one gainer is 'higher for longer' (up 207 percent on the quarter, velocity 38), not a word of reassurance.

pillars.title: The signal issue
pillars.body: What the inflation spike looks like through the velocity index — the highest-velocity terms against the declining ones, demonstrating the signal layer working in real time on the live print. At the top, 'vibecession' (velocity 100) and 'shrinkflation' (velocity 94); at the floor, 'tariff tax' (velocity 0, down 71 percent on the quarter) and 'last mile' (velocity 12, down 62 percent). The gap between them is the measured shape of a cycle where the mood is outrunning the metric — reported as velocity, never as a verdict on the print.

tensions.title: Soft landing vs vibecession
tensions.body: The cycle's defining collision, and it is measured. As inflation re-accelerated, the institutional-optimism term faded while the lived-pessimism term surged — the same data-turning producing opposite vocabulary movements. 'Vibecession' is the fastest mover in the set (velocity 100, up 573 percent over thirty days and up 7 percent on the quarter) while 'soft landing' has fallen to velocity 19, down 28 percent over ninety days. The vibe word is winning the argument the data word is presumed to be winning: the feeling is outrunning the rate.

tensions.title: Disinflation vs affordability
tensions.body: Rate versus level. 'Disinflation' is the technically precise term for prices rising more slowly; 'affordability' is the populist term for prices that are still high. Both describe the same economy truthfully with opposite emotional valence, and measured, both are cooling on the quarter — 'disinflation' down 28 percent (velocity 25, though up 46 percent in the last thirty) and 'affordability' down 13 percent (velocity 44). The institutional metric can improve every month while the populist metric never falls, and neither is the word carrying the cycle — that word is 'vibecession.'

tensions.title: Greedflation vs [admin]flation
tensions.body: Two attribution vocabularies competing to assign the cause of high prices — the firms or the government. Measured, the blame is migrating on the quarter: the corporation-blaming frame 'greedflation' is down 36 percent over ninety days (velocity 88, though it ticked up 11 percent in the last thirty), while the incumbent-blaming frame is up 90 percent over the same window (velocity 6, still rising off a small base). The blame is moving from the boardroom toward the ballot box as the midterms approach — with the caveat that the partisan frame is fast-rising, not yet loud, and the corporation frame is cooling from a still-high base rather than burned out.

tensions.title: K-shaped vs real wages
tensions.body: The institutional bridge. 'K-shaped' is analyst vocabulary that concedes the populist point — aggregate 'real wages' can rise while the median experience splits between asset-holders and wage-earners. Measured, both are among the sharpest thirty-day movers in the set: 'real wages' is up 96 percent over thirty days (velocity 75) and 'K-shaped' up 80 percent (velocity 69), even as both ease on the quarter. It is the rare institutional pair that validates the lived-experience complaint in the institutional cluster's own language — and that it is spiking now, as 'vibecession' tops the set, is the establishment vocabulary reaching for the words that admit the split.

tensions.title: Tariff tax vs soft landing
tensions.body: Is the policy a cost or a strategy — and here a measured number cuts against the tidy story. 'Tariff tax' reframes tariffs as a consumer tax paid at home, and the energy-and-tariff shock is precisely what ended the 'soft landing' narrative this cycle; yet 'tariff tax' has collapsed to the floor of the set (velocity 0, down 71 percent on the quarter) even as the cost it names is felt loudly through 'vibecession' and 'shrinkflation.' 'Soft landing' has faded too (velocity 19, down 28 percent). The lived cost is unmistakably the story; the specific partisan cost-label is not the word carrying it — the pain is named by the vibe vocabulary, not by the policy indictment. That divergence leads rather than hides.
